summary.text: Apply the positivity hypothesis at \(n=(M+2)!/6\) to obtain a Sophie Germain prime \(6x-1\) and a twin pair \(6y-1,6y+1\) with \((6x-1)+(6y+1)=(M+2)!\). If either family were finite, choose \(M\) bounding it; the relevant prime then divides the factorial and, by subtraction, the other prime, forcing equality—impossible since integers of the forms \(6x-1\) and \(6y+1\) cannot coincide.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) counts those integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\) for which, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Notice that if \(x\ge 1\), then
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say precisely that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Similarly,
\[
(6y-1)+2=6y+1,
\]
so the last two conditions say that \(6y-1\) and \(6y+1\) form a twin-prime pair.

Assume the conjectured positivity statement
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove that both \(S\) and \(T\) are infinite.

First observe what positivity gives. The definition of \(a(n)\) is a finite sum, over \(1\le x<n\), of terms that are either \(0\) or \(1\), with a term equal to \(1\) exactly when the four displayed numbers are prime. Therefore, if \(a(n)>0\), at least one summand is \(1\). Thus there is an integer \(x\) such that
\[
1\le x<n,
\]
and, with \(y=n-x\),
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Since \(x<n\), we also have \(y=n-x\ge1\), and of course \(x+y=n\).

We will use this observation with a specially chosen \(n\). The following construction will be common to both infinitude arguments. Let \(N\ge4\), and set
\[
F=(N+2)!.
\]
Because \(6\le N+2\), the integer \(6\) divides \((N+2)!\). Hence there is an integer \(n\) such that
\[
6n=F.
\]
Moreover, \(N+2\ge6\), so
\[
F=(N+2)!\ge6!=720,
\]
and consequently \(n\ge120>1\). The assumed positivity therefore applies to this \(n\). We obtain positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
x+y=n,
\]
all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are prime, and
\[
(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6x+6y=6(x+y)=6n=F=(N+2)!.
\tag{1}
\]
Thus, for every \(N\ge4\), we can decompose \((N+2)!\) as in (1), where the first summand is a Sophie Germain prime and the second summand is the upper member of a twin-prime pair.

We now prove that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(S\) is finite. Every finite set of natural numbers has an upper bound, so choose \(N_0\) such that
\[
p\le N_0\qquad\text{for every }p\in S.
\]
Put
\[
N=\max\{N_0,4\}.
\]
Then \(N\ge4\) and \(N_0\le N\). Apply the factorial construction above. We obtain positive integers \(x,y\) for which
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad q=6y+1
\]
are prime,
\[
12x-1=2p+1
\]
is prime, and
\[
p+q=(N+2)!.
\tag{2}
\]
Since both \(p\) and \(2p+1\) are prime, \(p\in S\). The assumed upper bound on \(S\) gives
\[
p\le N_0\le N<N+2.
\]
Also \(p>0\). Any positive integer at most \(N+2\) divides \((N+2)!\), because it occurs among the factors of that factorial. Hence
\[
p\mid (N+2)!.
\]
Together with (2), this implies
\[
p\mid q:
\]
indeed, \(p\) divides both \((N+2)!=p+q\) and \(p\), and therefore divides their difference \(q\).

But \(q\) is prime. The only positive divisors of a prime are \(1\) and the prime itself, so either
\[
p=1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
p=q.
\]
The first alternative is impossible because \(x\ge1\), and hence
\[
p=6x-1\ge5.
\]
The second alternative is also impossible: it would say
\[
6x-1=6y+1.
\]
Reducing this equality modulo \(6\) would give \(-1\equiv1\pmod 6\), or equivalently \(5\equiv1\pmod6\), which is false. Thus the assumption that \(S\) is finite leads to a contradiction. Therefore there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs. Recall that \(T\) records each pair by its lower member. Suppose, for contradiction, that \(T\) is finite. Choose an upper bound \(N_0\) for it, so that
\[
r\le N_0\qquad\text{for every }r\in T.
\]
Again put
\[
N=\max\{N_0,4\},
\]
and apply the same factorial construction. We obtain positive integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
p=6x-1,\qquad r=6y-1,\qquad q=6y+1=r+2
\]
are prime and
\[
p+q=(N+2)!.
\tag{3}
\]
Since \(r\) and \(r+2=q\) are both prime, \(r\in T\). Therefore
\[
r\le N_0\le N.
\]
It follows that the upper member of this twin-prime pair satisfies
\[
q=r+2\le N+2.
\]
As \(q>0\), the factorial divisibility property gives
\[
q\mid (N+2)!.
\]
Using (3), and subtracting the summand \(q\), we conclude that
\[
q\mid p.
\]
Now \(p\) is prime, so a positive divisor of \(p\) must be either \(1\) or \(p\). Consequently either
\[
q=1
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
q=p.
\]
The first alternative is impossible because \(y\ge1\) gives
\[
q=6y+1\ge7.
\]
The second is again impossible modulo \(6\), since
\[
p=6x-1\equiv5\pmod6,
\qquad
q=6y+1\equiv1\pmod6.
\]
This contradiction shows that \(T\) is infinite. Because each element of \(T\) uniquely represents the twin-prime pair \(\{r,r+2\}\), there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.

Hence the assumption that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies both that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
